name: Einstein Static Universe
description: Albert Einstein's cosmology of 1917: dust spread uniformly through a round three sphere of fixed radius and held at rest by a positive cosmological constant. Minkowski, de Sitter, and anti-de Sitter space are each conformal to a region of it.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the one parameter is the radius $R$ of the three sphere, a length. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history:
Albert Einstein presented the first relativistic cosmology to the Prussian Academy of Sciences on 8 February 1917 [einstein1917]. In Newton's theory a static universe can only be a finite island of stars in an infinite empty space, which by Boltzmann's statistics steadily loses its stars to infinity [einstein1917, oraifeartaigh2017]. Einstein wrote down the modified equation $
abla^2\phi - \lambda\phi = 4\pi Gho$, which allows a uniform distribution of matter through an infinite space [einstein1917]. He took the small relative velocities of the stars as the decisive fact and assumed a frame in which matter is permanently at rest, spread uniformly through a space closed into a three sphere of radius $R$, so that there is no boundary at infinity to set conditions on [einstein1917]. The field equations he had given the Academy in November 1915 admit no such world [einstein1915field], so he added the term $\lambda g_{\mu
u}$, with $\lambda$ a universal constant "at present unknown", and found every equation satisfied when $\lambda = \kappaho/2 = 1/R^2$, where $\kappa = 8\pi G/c^2$ [einstein1917]. The constant $\lambda$ fixes the density, the radius, and the total mass $M = 2\pi^2R^3ho$ at once [einstein1917].¶In letters of February and March 1917 to Paul Ehrenfest, Erwin Freundlich, Michele Besso, and Willem de Sitter, Einstein took a density of about $10^{-22}$ g/cm$^3$ from star counts and found a radius of about $10^7$ light years, a thousand times the $10^4$ light years then within reach of telescopes [oraifeartaigh2017]. Freundlich, Felix Klein, and de Sitter pointed out that the antipodal points of the three sphere can be identified, giving elliptic space of half the volume, and Einstein agreed, noting that his relation between $R$ and $ho$ was unchanged [oraifeartaigh2017]. The same world solves the field equations without the new term if the matter carries a constant negative pressure, as Erwin Schrödinger showed in 1918, and Einstein answered that the two formulations are equivalent [oraifeartaigh2017]. As Alex Harvey and Engelbert Schucking set out in 2000, in the Newtonian limit the amended field equations reduce to $
abla^2\phi + c^2\lambda = 4\pi Gho$, which adds a repulsion growing in proportion to distance, where Einstein had claimed a perfect analogy with his modified Poisson equation [harvey2000, oraifeartaigh2017].¶De Sitter found a second solution of the amended equations, empty of matter, and in November 1917 he called Einstein's world Solution A and his own Solution B [desitter1917, oraifeartaigh2017]. He estimated the radius of Einstein's world from the apparent diameters of astronomical objects, from the density of matter at the centre of the galaxy, and from the absence of an image of the Sun at its antipode, where the light the Sun sends out in every direction comes together again [oraifeartaigh2017]. Georges Lemaître found in 1927 an expanding universe that begins in the infinite past as an Einstein world of radius $R_0 = 1/\sqrt{\lambda}$, and read the recession of the spiral nebulae as its expansion [lemaitre1927, oraifeartaigh2017]. Arthur Eddington showed in 1930 that Einstein's world is unstable against a perturbation the same everywhere in space: a small fall in the density, with $\lambda$ held fixed, starts an expansion that runs away, and a small rise starts a collapse [eddington1930, oraifeartaigh2017]. He favoured a universe that had expanded from an Einstein world, the model known since as the Eddington-Lemaître universe [oraifeartaigh2017]. Einstein gave up the static world in April 1931, on the grounds that it is unstable and that Edwin Hubble's measurements of the recession of the nebulae left the assumption of a static space without justification, and dropped the cosmological constant with it [oraifeartaigh2014, oraifeartaigh2017].¶In an Einstein static universe filled with radiation every physical inhomogeneous mode oscillates, as Edward Harrison showed in 1967 [harrison1967, barrow2003]. Gary Gibbons proved in 1987 that one filled with a fluid is stable against conformal perturbations of its metric whenever the sound speed obeys $c_s^2 > c^2/5$ [gibbons1987, barrow2003]. John Barrow, George Ellis, Roy Maartens, and Christos Tsagas extended the analysis in 2003 to every scalar, vector, and tensor perturbation of a perfect fluid: the universe is neutrally stable against small vector and tensor inhomogeneities, and against adiabatic density inhomogeneities as long as $c_s^2 > c^2/5$, while homogeneous modes of Bianchi type IX destabilise it [barrow2003]. The stability comes from the closed space, which holds no wavelength longer than a maximum set by $R$, with the Jeans length a sizeable fraction of that maximum [barrow2003].¶George Ellis and Roy Maartens proposed in 2004 that our universe began as an Einstein static universe in the infinite past, then inflated and reheated into a hot big bang [ellis2004]. Such a universe has no singularity, no beginning of time, and no horizon problem, and if its initial radius lies above the Planck scale it has no era of quantum gravity, and classical general relativity describes it throughout [ellis2004]. Ellis, Jeff Murugan, and Christos Tsagas built one explicitly the same year, driven by a single scalar field with a physically based potential, which leaves the Einstein static state, inflates, reheats, and joins a standard hot big bang [ellis2004explicit]. Ellis, Murugan, and Tsagas called the emergent model "essentially a modified version of the Eddington-Lemaître universe" [ellis2004explicit].¶In his lectures at Les Houches in 1963, published in 1964, Roger Penrose mapped Minkowski space conformally onto a bounded region of the Einstein static universe, so that its infinity becomes a boundary at a finite place, which light rays reach [penrose1964conformal]. Stephen Hawking and George Ellis gave the corresponding conformal embeddings in 1973, in the conformal time $\eta = ct/R$, for de Sitter space, conformal to the region $-\pi/2 < \eta < \pi/2$ of the Einstein static universe, and for anti-de Sitter space, conformal to its half $0 \le \chi < \pi/2$, whose boundary is timelike [hawking1973]. On the strip $0 \le \chi \le \pi$ of the Einstein static universe, with light at 45°, the conformal diagram of Minkowski space is a triangle, that of de Sitter space a square, and that of anti-de Sitter space the half strip $\chi < \pi/2$ [hawking1973].

related.text: The static universe with its radius free to change in time. Einstein gave up the static one in 1931, starting from Friedmann's equations [oraifeartaigh2014].

The rival cosmology of 1917, Einstein's amended equations solved with no matter. Arthur Eddington summed up the pair as matter without motion and motion without matter [desitter1917, eddington1933]. It is conformal to the region $-\pi/2 < \eta < \pi/2$ of the static universe [hawking1973].
Roger Penrose mapped Minkowski space conformally onto a bounded region of the static universe in 1963, which brings its infinity to a finite place [penrose1964conformal].
Anti-de Sitter space is conformal to half of the static universe, $0 \le \chi < \pi/2$, and the equator where it ends is a timelike boundary [hawking1973].
A star of uniform density, inside which space is a cap of a three sphere, as Karl Schwarzschild found a year before Einstein's universe [schwarzschild1916b]. Einstein's space is the whole sphere.

Dust that rotates where Einstein's is at rest, held by a cosmological constant of the opposite sign. Kurt Gödel wrote in 1949, without proof, that his universe and Einstein's are the only spatially homogeneous solutions with matter whose world lines stay equidistant [godel1949].

A universe of radiation that also satisfies the strong energy condition and has no singularity, while it contracts, bounces, and expands. It has no compact slice and no point whose light cone converges again [senovilla1998, chinea1992].

coordinates.name: Hyperspherical

parameters.description: Radius of the three sphere, a length, which makes the time dimensionless as $\eta = ct/R$; for dust of density $\rho$ the field equations with a cosmological constant $\Lambda$ fix $\Lambda = 1/R^2$ and $\rho = c^2/(4\pi GR^2)$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \chi, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\chi$, $\theta$, and $\phi$ angles on the three sphere. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Areal
domains: r = R \;\text{(the equator of } S^3\text{; the coordinates cover one hemisphere)}

parameters.description: Radius of the three sphere, a length, which makes the time dimensionless as $\eta = ct/R$; for dust of density $\rho$ the field equations with a cosmological constant $\Lambda$ fix $\Lambda = 1/R^2$ and $\rho = c^2/(4\pi GR^2)$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r = R\sin\chi$ the areal radius, which covers the hemisphere $\chi < \pi/2$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Einstein's Cartesian
domains: x^2 + y^2 + z^2 < R^2 \;\text{(one hemisphere of } S^3\text{)}

parameters.description: Radius of the three sphere, a length, which makes the time dimensionless as $\eta = ct/R$; for dust of density $\rho$ the field equations with a cosmological constant $\Lambda$ fix $\Lambda = 1/R^2$ and $\rho = c^2/(4\pi GR^2)$

coordinates.convention: We use Albert Einstein's coordinates of 1917, $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$, $y$, and $z$ the lengths of the projection of the hemisphere $\chi < \pi/2$ onto its equatorial plane. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
coordinates.line_element: ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 + \dfrac{\left(x\,dx + y\,dy + z\,dz\right)^2}{R^2 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2}
